The first surveys of the valley were made in the summer of 1873, by a team of four who had been told to expect three weeks of work and stayed for nine. Their notebooks, which survive almost complete, record the weather every morning, the condition of the pack animals, and — with a thoroughness that later readers have found both useful and slightly maddening — the price of every meal they bought along the way. What the notebooks do not record, anywhere, is why the survey was commissioned. The official file was lost in a fire at the regional office in 1904, and the correspondence that might have explained it was, by all accounts, never copied. Historians have proposed three explanations. The first is that the survey was routine, one of dozens ordered that decade, and that its file was simply unremarkable. The second is that it was connected to a mineral claim which was later abandoned, and that the paperwork was deliberately allowed to lapse. The third, and the least supported, is that the survey was a pretext for something else entirely. What is certain is that the maps produced that summer remained in use for over forty years, and that at least two of the four surveyors never worked in the field again.

Consider a system that processes eighty items per second at steady state. If each item requires four sequential stages, and each stage takes an average of three milliseconds, then the naive expectation is a throughput ceiling near eighty-three items per second — which is close enough to the observed figure that it invites the wrong conclusion. The wrong conclusion is that the system is near its limit. In fact the four stages do not contend for the same resource. Stages one and three are bound by memory bandwidth; stages two and four are bound by a single lock. Measured separately, the lock is held for one point one milliseconds per item, which places a hard ceiling at roughly nine hundred items per second, while the memory path saturates at about one hundred and forty. The binding constraint, therefore, is memory, and the lock — the thing everyone assumed was the problem, because locks usually are — has more than six times the headroom it needs. Removing it would buy nothing. This is worth stating plainly because the team spent five weeks removing it.

对这片山谷最早的勘测是在一八七三年夏天完成的，勘测队一共四个人，出发时被告知工作大约需要三周，结果待了九周。他们的笔记本几乎完整地保存了下来，里面记录了每天早晨的天气、驮畜的状况，以及——后来的读者觉得既有用又有点让人恼火的详尽程度——沿途每一顿饭的价钱。笔记本里唯独没有记录的，是这次勘测究竟因何而起。官方档案在一九零四年地区办事处的一场火灾中遗失，可能解释缘由的往来信件，据说从未抄录副本。历史学者提出过三种说法。第一种认为这只是例行勘测，那十年里下达过几十次，档案本身平淡无奇。第二种认为它与一项后来被放弃的矿权申请有关，文件因此被有意搁置。第三种说法证据最少，认为勘测只是某件别的事情的借口。可以确定的是，那年夏天绘制的地图此后沿用了四十多年，而四位勘测者中至少有两人再也没有回到野外工作。

Los primeros reconocimientos del valle se hicieron en el verano de 1873, a cargo de un equipo de cuatro personas a las que se les había dicho que el trabajo duraría tres semanas y que permanecieron nueve. Sus cuadernos, conservados casi completos, registran el tiempo cada mañana, el estado de las bestias de carga y, con una minuciosidad que los lectores posteriores han encontrado a la vez útil y algo exasperante, el precio de cada comida que compraron por el camino. Lo que los cuadernos no registran en ningún sitio es por qué se encargó el reconocimiento. El expediente oficial se perdió en un incendio en la oficina regional en 1904, y la correspondencia que podría haberlo explicado nunca llegó a copiarse. Lo que sí es seguro es que los mapas trazados aquel verano siguieron usándose durante más de cuarenta años.
